while the 0-1 principle requires the network to sort all 8192 binary vectors simultaneously, so the pruning condition must hold for every vector, not just one."],"overturn_conditions":["If the nodes / total nodes) is below 5% for n=12, the rule is practically useless and the claim of 'measurable fraction' is overturned."],"shared_structure":["Both domains have a fixed budget (comparator exponentially large input space (binary vectors / permutations) to admit or reject complete solutions.","Both feature symmetry reduction (reflection of channel indices / reversal of permutation positions) that halves the effective search space without losing optimality."],"source_memory_refs":["branch_and_bound_inversion_bound_for_permutation_sorting"],"transfer_claims":["Just as branch-and-bound with inversion-count lower bounds prunes provably-suboptimal branches in permutation sorting without losing the optimum, the per-vector inversion-budget pruning rule should preserve at least one optimal S(n)-comparator network for n\u226412.","The measured pruning ratio (fraction of nodes cut) in the permutation-sorting analogy correlates with the pruning ratio expected in the sorting-network search, suggesting the rule is useful when the ratio exceeds ~30%."]},"claim":"A lower-bound-admissible prefix-pruning rule \u2014 reject any partial comparator network at depth k (out of budget B) if there exists a binary input vector in {0,1}^13 whose image under the prefix has more than B\u2212k inversions among the 1-bits, since each remaining comparator can fix at most one such inversion \u2014 preserves at least one optimal solution for all proven cases (n\u226412) and, applied to the S(13)\u226445 search, will prune a measurable fraction of the search tree without losing the known 45-comparator solution class.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The inversion-count bound may be too weak to prune meaningfully: in practice many prefixes with \u2264B\u2212k inversions are still uncompletable, so the pruning ratio could be negligible and the rule would not discriminate from brute-force search.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The bound could be unsound if the definition of 'inversion' does not correctly capture the minimum number of comparators needed to sort a binary vector \u2014 e.g., a single comparator can fix multiple inversions if channels are reused, but in a straight-line network each comparator acts on a fixed pair, so this is unlikely; still, the simulation must verify no false prunes.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The pruning rule may preserve under a fixed node budget) may show no wall-clock advantage despite a smaller effective branching factor.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By the 0-1 principle (block b01150a3ae43d8f6), verifying a 13-input network requires checking all 8192 binary vectors (block 6050cf69f391fa33). Each comparator (i,j) in a network can reduce the total number of inversions in a binary output vector by at most one: it swaps when channel i has a 1 and channel j has a 0, turning that inversion into a correct ordering. Thus, after placing k of B comparators, if any binary vector's image under the prefix still has strictly more than B\u2212k inversions among pairs (i,j) with i<j, the prefix can never be completed to a valid sorter within budget, regardless of which comparators are appended. This bound is admissible (never prunes a valid completable prefix) because it is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The simulation tests this on n=10, 11, 12 where S(n) is known (block 8a7a7d8f89f48b3e): run depth-first search with and without the pruning rule under budget S(n) and confirm the pruned search still finds a valid S(n)-comparator network, then measure the pruning ratio.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
